summary: An overview of a routing workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board in March 1998. It records the discussions on the state and problems of Internet routing and what the community thought should be worked on next.

plainLanguage.summary: Some experts met for three days to talk about how Internet traffic finds its way. This is the written report of what they said.

subtitle: Documenting Internet routing challenges and solutions from a 1998 expert workshop.

tldr.problem: The Internet routing system faced scaling challenges, instability, and limitations that threatened its future growth. Experts needed to align on what should be done next.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board held a three-day workshop in March 1998 to discuss routing problems, current approaches, and necessary research directions across multiple technical areas.
tldr.outcome: The workshop produced conclusions and action items covering unicast routing, multicast, address translation, quality of service, security, policy, and network management—all still relevant to Internet infrastructure work.

facts.label: Primary focus
facts.value: Unicast routing scaling, multicast routing, routing stability

today: RFC 2902 is an Informational document recording a specific moment in Internet history. The routing challenges identified in 1998 (scaling, multicast efficiency, security, policy coordination) remain relevant to modern network infrastructure. Some recommendations led to ongoing research efforts and working group activities.

sections.title: The 1998 Routing Workshop
sections.content:
In March 1998, the Internet Architecture Board brought together leading experts to review how Internet routing worked and what challenges lay ahead. The workshop brought together voices from router vendors, Internet service providers, research institutions, and standards organizations to tackle fundamental questions about the Internet's architecture.

This document records what that group discussed and concluded. Rather than offering final answers, the workshop explored expert intuition built from years of experience running the Internet, and pointed to areas needing deeper research and engineering work.
sections.plainLanguage: Experts met to talk about how the Internet finds a path for data. They wrote down what they talked about and what they thought should happen next.

sections.title: The Core Routing Challenges
sections.content:
The workshop examined eight major technical topics. The most serious was the scaling of unicast routing and IP address allocation. Experts agreed that most immediate stability problems could be fixed with better router implementations, but long-term systemic issues like flapping (rapid route changes) and multi-homing (connecting through multiple providers) would only worsen without new approaches.

The group also discussed whether the Internet needed more levels of hierarchy in its routing tables and addresses. The conclusion was that flat routing at the autonomous system level remained workable, but only if addressed carefully to manage convergence time and trust relationships.

Network Address Translation boxes—devices that let private networks share a single public address—raised concerns. While widely deployed, they created problems with how applications and routing interacted, prompting discussion of whether to eliminate, fix, or work around them.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers were sending too many route changes and getting confused about which way to send traffic. Some networks were trying to use tricks to get around address shortages, but those tricks had their own problems.

sections.title: Multicast, Quality of Service, and Network Stability
sections.content:
The workshop examined multicast routing—the ability to send one message to many receivers efficiently. Experts noted that existing multicast protocols worked well in some scenarios but scaled poorly when applications had different requirements: varying numbers of sources and receivers, different group sizes, different topological spans, and high membership churn.

Quality of Service, Class of Service, and Type of Service terminology was muddled. The group defined these terms precisely (Type of Service as hop-by-hop routing based on destination and ToS bits; Class of Service as service contracts; Quality of Service as meeting specific constraints) and discussed the emerging concept of constraint-based routing—using traffic engineering on large aggregated flows to help providers manage bandwidth allocation.

Routing stability merited continued research. The group found that damping route updates improved stability but could temporarily hide prefixes from some networks. Roughly 1% of prefixes showed signs of dampening at any given time, but measuring how many became unreachable was needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending one message to many places works in some cases but not others. Nobody agreed on what "good quality" meant for routing. Route flapping could be calmed down, but sometimes that made things disappear.

sections.title: Security and Policy
sections.content:
Routing security required routers with security as good as any host computer. The group emphasized that one compromised router could cause widespread damage, and console access gave complete control. Providers should consider taking control traffic out of band due to lack of wire-speed authentication.

Border Gateway Protocol policy management was identified as fragile and error-prone. Some ISP routing policies were unsolvable with BGP alone. Router configuration languages were complex and hard to get right. The group concluded the Internet needed a better routing policy specification language and encouraged work on wire-speed authentication and Byzantine robustness in routing protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need strong security because one bad router can break everything. Setting router policies is complicated and easy to mess up.

sections.title: Network Information and Emerging Areas
sections.content:
The workshop discussed information flowing from the network to applications. Publishing traffic statistics along backbone routes could help services choose the best cache location. Web browsers and other applications wanted to auto-discover local caches instead of being hard-coded. The group recommended a Birds of a Feather session on measuring path characteristics and consideration by the IPPM working group.

Several shorter topics received attention: multi-strand trunking (treating parallel network links as one link with richer metrics), better diagnostic tools and monitoring, anycast addressing, load-sensitive routing, geographical addressing, and renumbering. Each topic spawned specific recommendations for research groups or working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications should know which nearby servers have data cached. Several other ideas came up that needed more study.

sections.title: Action Items and Legacy
sections.content:
The workshop produced action items for the IAB, IETF working group chairs, and the IRTF Routing Research Group. The IAB was asked to continue being concerned about NAT issues and promote better diagnostic tools. IETF groups received guidance on constraint-based routing, routing security work, policy language concerns, multicast evaluation, and anycast research. The IRTF was encouraged to analyze routing data more deeply, evaluate multicast mechanisms, and study load-sensitive routing.

These recommendations shaped routing and network research for years after the workshop. While the specific technologies discussed have evolved, the fundamental challenges—scaling routing systems, managing address allocation, balancing performance and security, and coordinating policy across domains—remain relevant to modern Internet infrastructure work.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop made a list of things different groups should work on. Some became important Internet technologies, and some challenges are still being solved today.
